items.stem: What is the phase difference between two points on a progressive wave that are half a wavelength apart?
items.answer: 180° (π rad)
items.markingKey: Phase difference = 360° × Δx/λ = 180°.

items.stem: Derive v = fλ from the definitions of frequency and wavelength.
items.answer: In one period T the wave travels one wavelength λ, so v = λ/T; since f = 1/T, v = fλ.
items.markingKey: distance λ in time T [1]; T = 1/f gives v = fλ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, giving an example of each.
items.answer: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string); longitudinal: oscillations parallel to energy transfer (e.g. sound).
items.markingKey: transverse definition with example [1]; longitudinal definition with example [1] [2]

items.stem: A microphone connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope detects a sound wave. One complete wave occupies 4.0 divisions horizontally; the time-base is set at 5.0 ms div⁻¹. Calculate the frequency of the sound.
items.answer: 50 Hz
items.markingKey: T = 4.0 × 5.0 ms = 20 ms; f = 1/T = 50 Hz. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A microphone connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope detects a sound wave. One complete wave occupies 2.5 divisions horizontally; the time-base is set at 5.0 ms div⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency and the wavelength.

A vibration generator sends transverse waves of frequency 2.0 Hz, wavelength 2.0 cm and amplitude 3.0 mm along a long spring. (a) Calculate the phase difference between two points 0.50 cm apart. (b) Explain how the wave transfers energy without transferring matter.
items.answer: (a) 90° (π/2 rad) (b) Each particle oscillates about its equilibrium position, passing energy to neighbouring particles.
items.markingKey: (a) separation = λ/4 [1]; phase difference = 360° × ¼ = 90° [1] [2] (b) oscillation about fixed position [1]; energy passed on [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium oscillate … (b) Which is the definition of wavelength?
items.answer: (a) parallel to the direction of energy transfer (b) The minimum distance between two points on a wave that are in phase
items.markingKey: (a) Compressions and rarefactions form along the direction of travel. (b) For example, crest to adjacent crest.

items.stem: Explain how a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) trace can be used to find the frequency of a sound wave.
items.answer: Measure the horizontal length of one (or several) complete cycles in divisions; multiply by the time-base setting to get the period T; f = 1/T.
items.markingKey: measure divisions for a cycle [1]; × time-base gives T [1]; f = 1/T [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why points on a progressive wave one wavelength apart oscillate in phase.
items.answer: The wave pattern repeats every wavelength, so the two points have the same displacement and velocity at all times.
items.markingKey: pattern repeats each λ [1]; same displacement and motion at every instant [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, giving an example of each. (b) Derive v = fλ from the definitions of frequency and wavelength.
items.answer: (a) Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string); longitudinal: oscillations parallel to energy transfer (e.g. sound). (b) In one period T the wave travels one wavelength λ, so v = λ/T; since f = 1/T, v = fλ.
items.markingKey: (a) transverse definition with example [1]; longitudinal definition with example [1] [2] (b) distance λ in time T [1]; T = 1/f gives v = fλ [1] [2]

items.stem: A progressive wave has wavelength 2.0 m. Two points P and Q on the wave are 1.0 m apart along the direction of travel. Calculate the phase difference between P and Q in degrees.
items.markingKey: φ = 360° × 1.0/2.0 = 180°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A wave of frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 0.80 m travels along a rope. (a) Calculate the wave speed. (b) Calculate the phase difference, in radians, between two points 0.40 m apart. (c) Calculate the phase difference at one point between times separated by 5.0 ms.
items.answer: (a) 40 m s⁻¹ (b) 1.0π rad (c) 0.50π rad

items.stem: A microphone connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope detects a sound wave. One complete wave occupies 5.0 divisions horizontally; the time-base is set at 0.50 ms div⁻¹. The trace has a peak-to-peak height of 3.0 divisions and the y-gain is 2.0 mV div⁻¹. (a) Calculate the frequency. (b) Calculate the amplitude of the signal. (c) Describe the change to the trace if the frequency is doubled with the same amplitude.
items.answer: (a) 400 Hz (b) 3.0 mV (c) twice as many cycles on the screen (each cycle occupies 2.5 divisions); height unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 2.5 ms [1]; f = 400 Hz [1] (b) amplitude = 1.5 div × 2.0 mV div⁻¹ = 3.0 mV [1] (c) cycles halve in width [1]; height unchanged [1] [5]

items.stem: A vibration generator sends transverse waves of frequency 5.0 Hz, wavelength 2.5 cm and amplitude 4.0 mm along a long spring. (a) Calculate the phase difference between two points 0.625 cm apart. (b) Calculate the total distance moved by a particle on the wave in 1.0 s.
items.markingKey: (a) separation = λ/4 [1]; phase difference = 360° × ¼ = 90° [1] [2] (b) 4A per cycle × f (method/substitution) [1]; answer 80 mm with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the definition of intensity of a wave?
options: Power per unit area perpendicular to the direction of travel
items.answer: Power per unit area perpendicular to the direction of travel
items.markingKey: I = P/A, unit W m⁻².

items.stem: The amplitude of a wave is doubled. The intensity …
items.answer: is multiplied by 4
items.markingKey: I ∝ A².

items.stem: Explain why the intensity of sound from a small source decreases with distance.
items.answer: The power spreads over the surface of an ever larger sphere (area 4πr²), so the power per unit area falls as 1/r² (ignoring absorption).
items.markingKey: power spread over larger area [1]; I = P/(4πr²) ∝ 1/r² [1] [2]

items.stem: A siren on a pole emits sound uniformly in all directions with a power of 2.0 W. Work out the intensity at a distance of 5.0 m.
items.markingKey: I = P/(4πr²) = 2.0/(4π × 5.0²) = 0.00637 W m⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A point source of sound of power 4.0 W is placed in an open field. (a) Define intensity. (b) Explain why the intensity falls with distance.
items.answer: (a) Power per unit area (normal to the direction of travel). (b) Power spreads over a larger spherical area 4πr².
items.markingKey: (a) Power per unit area (normal to the direction of travel) [1] (b) larger area [1]; inverse square [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the intensity of a laser beam hardly decreases over a short distance.
items.answer: The beam does not spread out much, so the area over which the power is spread stays almost constant.
items.markingKey: little spreading [1]; area constant so I constant [1] [2]

items.stem: A small lamp radiates light uniformly in all directions with a power of 5.0 W. Calculate the intensity at 2.0 m and at 6.0 m, and state the ratio of the intensities.
items.markingKey: I = P/(4πr²) = 0.0995 W m⁻² [1]; at 6.0 m: 0.0111 W m⁻² [1]; ratio 9 (inverse square) [1] [3]

items.stem: A small lamp radiates light uniformly in all directions with a power of 100 W. At 10 m the amplitude of the wave is 2.0 µm. (a) Calculate the intensity at 10 m. (b) Calculate the distance at which the intensity is a quarter of this. (c) Calculate the amplitude at that distance.
items.markingKey: (a) I = P/(4πr²) = 0.0796 W m⁻² [1] (b) I ∝ 1/r² so r doubles: 20 m [1] (c) I ∝ A² so A halves [1]; = 1.0 µm [1] [4]

items.stem: A small speaker at an outdoor concert in Nairobi radiates 2.0 W of sound uniformly in all directions. (a) Define intensity. (b) Calculate the ratio of the amplitudes at 2.0 m and 4.0 m.
items.answer: (a) Power per unit area (normal to the direction of travel). (b) 2 : 1
items.markingKey: (a) Power per unit area (normal to the direction of travel) [1] (b) I ∝ 1/r² so intensity ratio 4 : 1 [1]; A ∝ √I gives 2 : 1 [1] [2]

items.stem: A point source of sound of power 4.0 W is placed in an open field. (a) Define intensity. (b) Calculate the intensity at 3.0 m. (c) Calculate the ratio of the amplitudes at 3.0 m and 6.0 m.
items.answer: (a) Power per unit area (normal to the direction of travel). (b) 0.0354 W m⁻² (c) 2 : 1
items.markingKey: (a) Power per unit area (normal to the direction of travel) [1] (b) I = P/(4πr²) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.0354 W m⁻² with unit [1] [2] (c) I ∝ 1/r² so intensity ratio 4 : 1 [1]; A ∝ √I gives 2 : 1 [1] [2]

items.stem: A source of sound moves towards a stationary observer. The observed frequency is …
items.answer: higher than the source frequency
items.markingKey: Wavefronts are bunched ahead of the moving source, so λ decreases and f increases.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why the frequency heard from an approaching source is higher than the emitted frequency.
items.answer: The source moves towards the observer between emitting successive wavefronts, so they are closer together (shorter λ); the wave speed is unchanged so more wavefronts arrive per second.
items.markingKey: source moves between emissions [1]; λ shorter [1]; same v so higher f [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the speed of the sound waves is not changed by the motion of the source.
items.answer: The speed of sound depends only on the medium (air) and its conditions, not on the motion of the source.
items.markingKey: speed set by medium [1]

items.stem: A racing car engine note emits sound of frequency 600 Hz while moving at 30 m s⁻¹ away from a stationary observer. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard by the observer.
items.answer: 551 Hz
items.markingKey: f₀ = f_s v/(v + v_s) = 600 × 340/(340 + 30) = 551 Hz. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A police car siren of frequency 1200 Hz passes a stationary observer at a constant 25 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequencies heard as it approaches and as it recedes.
items.answer: 1300 Hz approaching; 1120 Hz receding
items.markingKey: approaching f_s v/(v − v_s) = 1300 Hz [1]; receding f_s v/(v + v_s) = 1120 Hz [1]; correct assignment [1] [3]

items.stem: A model aircraft emitting a 900 Hz tone flies past a microphone at 30 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the frequency heard as the source approaches. (b) Calculate the wavelength of the sound in front of the source.
items.markingKey: (a) f_s v/(v − v_s) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 987 Hz with unit [1] [2] (b) λ = (v − v_s)/f_s (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.344 m with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State what is meant by the Doppler effect. (b) As an ambulance passes a pedestrian, the pitch of its siren appears to …
items.answer: (a) The change in observed frequency of a wave when the source moves relative to the observer. (b) fall
items.markingKey: (a) change in observed frequency due to relative motion [1] (b) Approaching: higher f; receding: lower f.

items.stem: Describe how the frequency heard by a stationary observer changes as a train sounding its horn passes at constant speed.
items.answer: Higher than emitted as it approaches (constant), drops quickly as it passes, then constant and lower than emitted as it recedes.
items.markingKey: higher on approach [1]; lower when receding with sudden drop [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why the frequency heard from an approaching source is higher than the emitted frequency. (b) Explain why the speed of the sound waves is not changed by the motion of the source.
items.answer: (a) The source moves towards the observer between emitting successive wavefronts, so they are closer together (shorter λ); the wave speed is unchanged so more wavefronts arrive per second. (b) The speed of sound depends only on the medium (air) and its conditions, not on the motion of the source.
items.markingKey: (a) source moves between emissions [1]; λ shorter [1]; same v so higher f [1] [3] (b) speed set by medium [1]

items.stem: A police car siren emits sound of frequency 400 Hz while moving at 30 m s⁻¹ towards a stationary observer. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency heard by the observer?
items.answer: 440 Hz

items.stem: An ambulance siren emits sound of frequency 1200 Hz while moving at 10 m s⁻¹ towards a stationary observer. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Work out the frequency heard by the observer.
items.markingKey: f₀ = f_s v/(v − v_s) = 1200 × 340/(340 − 10) = 1240 Hz. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An ambulance siren of frequency 500 Hz passes a stationary observer at a constant 25 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequencies heard as it approaches and as it recedes.

items.stem: An observer by a straight road in Seoul hears a train horn at 425 Hz as it approaches and 378 Hz as it moves away at the same speed. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Determine the speed of the source and the frequency it emits.
items.answer: v_s = 19.9 m s⁻¹; f_s = 400 Hz

items.stem: What is the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum?
items.markingKey: c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ for all EM waves.

items.stem: Explain why electromagnetic waves can be polarised but sound waves in air cannot.
items.answer: EM waves are transverse (the oscillations can be restricted to one plane); sound in air is longitudinal, with oscillations along the direction of travel.
items.markingKey: EM transverse [1]; sound longitudinal [1] [2]

items.stem: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves and one property that differs between regions.
items.answer: Shared: transverse, travel at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum, need no medium; different: wavelength/frequency (and photon energy).
items.markingKey: two shared properties [1]; differing property [1] [2]

items.stem: A green laser emits light of frequency 563 THz. Work out the wavelength in a vacuum.
items.markingKey: λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸/5.63 × 10¹⁴ = 5.33 × 10⁻⁷ m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A Wi-Fi router transmits at 2.4 GHz. Calculate the wavelength of the signal and the time taken for an electromagnetic signal to travel from Earth to the Sun, a distance of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m.

items.markingKey: finite speed c [1]; delay from distance/c [1] [2]

items.stem: Which type of wave can be polarised?
items.answer: Transverse waves only
items.markingKey: Polarisation restricts oscillations to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel.

items.stem: Plane-polarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polariser whose transmission axis is at angle θ to the plane of polarisation. What is the transmitted intensity (Malus's law)?
items.answer: I₀ cos² θ
items.markingKey: Malus's law: I = I₀ cos² θ.

items.stem: Explain why polarisation provides evidence that light is a transverse wave.
items.answer: Only transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel that can be restricted to one plane; light can be polarised (blocked by crossed polaroids), so it must be transverse.
items.markingKey: polarisation only possible for transverse [1]; light is polarised by filters [1] [2]

items.stem: Plane-polarised light of intensity 6.0 W m⁻² is incident on a polarising filter whose transmission axis is at 40° to the plane of polarisation. Determine the transmitted intensity.
items.markingKey: I = I₀ cos² θ = 6.0 × cos² 40° = 3.52 W m⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student in a practical class in Bogotá shines unpolarised light of intensity 16 W m⁻² through two polarising filters, P and Q, and onto a light sensor. (a) State Malus's law. (b) Explain why this experiment shows light is a transverse wave.
items.answer: (a) I = I₀ cos² θ, where θ is the angle between the plane of polarisation and the transmission axis. (b) Intensity falls to zero when the filters are crossed; only transverse waves can be polarised.
items.markingKey: (a) I = I₀ cos² θ, where θ is the angle between the plane of polarisation and the transmission axis [1] (b) zero when crossed [1]; transverse only [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe what is seen when an analyser is rotated through 360° in front of a beam of plane-polarised light.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why there is a time delay in a radio conversation with astronauts on the Moon. (b) Explain why electromagnetic waves can be polarised but sound waves in air cannot.
items.answer: (a) Radio waves travel at a finite speed c; the Moon is about 3.8 × 10⁸ m away, so each signal takes about 1.3 s. (b) EM waves are transverse (the oscillations can be restricted to one plane); sound in air is longitudinal, with oscillations along the direction of travel.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Derive v = fλ from the definitions of frequency and wavelength. (b) Explain how a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) trace can be used to find the frequency of a sound wave.
items.answer: (a) In one period T the wave travels one wavelength λ, so v = λ/T; since f = 1/T, v = fλ. (b) Measure the horizontal length of one (or several) complete cycles in divisions; multiply by the time-base setting to get the period T; f = 1/T.
items.markingKey: (a) distance λ in time T [1]; T = 1/f gives v = fλ [1] [2] (b) measure divisions for a cycle [1]; × time-base gives T [1]; f = 1/T [1] [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the intensity of a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude. (b) Explain why the intensity of a laser beam hardly decreases over a short distance.
items.answer: (a) Energy of an oscillating particle ∝ (amplitude)²; intensity is the rate of energy transfer per unit area, so I ∝ A². (b) The beam does not spread out much, so the area over which the power is spread stays almost constant.
items.markingKey: (a) energy ∝ A² [1]; intensity ∝ energy transfer rate [1] [2] (b) little spreading [1]; area constant so I constant [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the speed of the sound waves is not changed by the motion of the source. (b) Describe how the frequency heard by a stationary observer changes as a train sounding its horn passes at constant speed.
items.answer: (a) The speed of sound depends only on the medium (air) and its conditions, not on the motion of the source. (b) Higher than emitted as it approaches (constant), drops quickly as it passes, then constant and lower than emitted as it recedes.
items.markingKey: (a) speed set by medium [1] (b) higher on approach [1]; lower when receding with sudden drop [1] [2]
